title: Lens

notes.heading: 1. Lensmaker's Formula, Thin-Lens Equation & Medium Immersion
notes.proseLatex: For a thin lens of glass index $n_g$ immersed in a surrounding medium $n_m$, Lensmaker's formula gives $\frac{1}{f} = \left(\frac{n_g}{n_m} - 1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$ (for equiconvex in air: $R_1 = +R,\; R_2 = -R \implies \frac{1}{f} = \frac{2(n_g-1)}{R}$). Notice if $n_m > n_g$ (e.g., air bubble or crown glass in $\text{CS}_2$), the sign flips so a convex lens behaves as a DIVERGING lens! The paraxial thin-lens formula is $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ with magnification $m = +\frac{v}{u} = \frac{f}{f + u}$.

keyFormulas.label: Lensmaker's Formula & Thin-Lens Equation
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Predict focal-length scaling in liquids and compute real/virtual image positions.

examples.problemLatex: A convex glass lens ($n_g = 1.5$) has focal length $f_a = +20\text{ cm}$ in air. Find its focal length $f_w$ when immersed in water ($n_w = 4/3$).
stepsLatex: Hence $f_w = 4 \times 20\text{ cm} = +80\text{ cm}$ (always quadruples for $n_g=3/2$ in water $n_w=4/3$!).

notes.heading: 2. Cutting a Lens & Minimum Screen Distance (D ≥ 4f)
notes.proseLatex: Cutting an equiconvex lens (focal length $f$) TRANSVERSELY along its vertical diameter into two plano-convex halves DOUBLES each piece's focal length to $2f$ (power halves); cutting HORIZONTALLY along the principal axis leaves focal length UNCHANGED at $f$ (only image brightness drops as aperture area halves!). Between a real object and a real screen image formed by a converging lens, minimum separation is $D_{\min} = 4f$, and for $D > 4f$ the displacement method gives $f = \frac{D^2 - d^2}{4D}$.

keyFormulas.label: Minimum Real Object-Image Distance & Displacement Method
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Apply D >= 4f and the two-position displacement method.

notes.heading: 3. Optical Power (Dioptre), Coaxial Combinations & Silvered Lenses
notes.proseLatex: Optical power is $P = \frac{1}{f(\text{in metres})} = \frac{100}{f(\text{in cm})}$ dioptres ($\text{D}$). Two coaxial thin lenses separated by $d$ combine with $P_{\text{eq}} = P_1 + P_2 - d P_1 P_2$ (in contact $d=0$: $P_{\text{eq}} = P_1 + P_2$ and $m_{\text{eq}} = m_1 m_2$). Silvering one face of a thin lens turns the system into an equivalent spherical MIRROR satisfying $\frac{1}{F_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{f_m} - \frac{2}{f_L}$ (in magnitude: $P_{\text{eq}} = 2P_{\text{lens}} + P_{\text{mirror}}$).

keyFormulas.label: Optical Power, Separated Lenses & Silvered Lens
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Add dioptre powers of contact/separated lenses and solve silvered-lens mirrors.

examples.problemLatex: A thin convex lens ($f_1 = +25\text{ cm}$) and a thin concave lens ($f_2 = -50\text{ cm}$) are placed in contact. Find equivalent power and focal length.

wbjeebTraps: Dioptre unit trap: $P = 1/f$ requires $f$ in METRES (so $f = +20\text{ cm} \implies P = +5\text{ D}$, NOT $+0.05\text{ D}$!).
Lens magnification is $m = +\frac{v}{u}$ (NO minus sign, unlike mirrors $m = -\frac{v}{u}$!).
Painting black half the aperture of a lens STILL forms a COMPLETE image of the object — only image intensity drops.
